title: Guests with news
hook: angels visit Ibrahim, he hurries to feed them, and his wife laughs at the news of a son

segments.voice: Yesterday: khalil, the friend of Allah, the name Ibrahim carries. Your line was a friend listens.

The doorbell rings, and nobody was expected. A quick inventory starts: anything in the fridge? Laundry on the couch? Ibrahim, peace be upon him, gets that doorbell. Strangers arrive at his tent. They say peace, and he says peace back. He doesn't know who they are. He doesn't ask what they want. The Qur'an says he slipped away to his household, quietly, and came back with a whole roasted calf. Not a snack. A feast, for people he'd never met. Then something strange happens. The guests don't eat. Their hands don't reach for the food.
screen: `STRANGERS AT THE TENT.` → `A WHOLE ROASTED CALF.` → `THEIR HANDS DON'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an tells this story twice, in Surah Hud and in Surah adh-Dhariyat, and each telling adds a detail. Surah Hud says he did not delay. Adh-Dhariyat says he went to his family quietly, so the guests wouldn't feel like a burden, brought a fat calf and set it close to them. Then, gently: won't you eat? That's hospitality in two verses: hurry, don't make a fuss, put the best you have within reach. The Qur'an calls them the honored guests of Ibrahim, and the honor starts with the host. They don't eat, and Ibrahim feels a flicker of fear. Commentators explain that in his world, a guest who refused your food might mean you harm. They say, don't be afraid. They're messengers, angels, sent on to the people of Lut, with news for this house. His wife is standing nearby. The Qur'an doesn't name her; Muslim tradition knows her as Sarah. She laughs. How can I bear a child, an old woman, with a husband this old? The angels answer: are you amazed at the command of Allah? A son is coming, Ishaq, and after him a grandson, Ya'qub. Commentators don't agree why she laughed: the surprise, relief, the sheer impossibility. The text leaves it open. Jews and Christians tell this visit too, at the oaks of Mamre in Genesis. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made the host's side part of faith: a hadith in Bukhari says whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let them honor their guest. Ibrahim fed strangers before he knew they carried good news. The feeding came first.
screen: `HE DID NOT DELAY.` · `THE HONORED GUESTS OF IBRAHIM.` · `THE GUESTS DON'T EAT.` · `SHE LAUGHS AT THE NEWS.` · then, large: `HONOR YOUR GUEST.`

segments.voice: Picture the people you'll cross paths with before tonight, a roommate, a coworker, a kid, and pick one. Now picture what you could put within their reach: a coffee, half your lunch, a plate saved for later; Ibrahim brought a fat calf, and yours can be the best you have today, even if it's a granola bar. If you pray, you can ask for an open hand.
Dayf, guest: the honored strangers Ibrahim fed before he knew they carried news of a son.
Your line: hurry to the guest. In Ibrahim's tent, the food came before the questions. That's day thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Welcoming guests with food and drink is a familiar part of Muslim home life, and teachers often cite the hadith about honoring the guest as the reason.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 51:24: "the honored guests of Ibrahim." dayf means guest.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about angels.
what it means: a story about a host. Ibrahim feeds strangers at once and well, before he knows they carry news of a son.
what a scholar hears: al-mukramin, "the honored": commentators read it both ways, guests honored by Allah and guests honored by Ibrahim's welcome.
recall: the name tradition gives Nuh's son

notes: The index word here is the title head "Guests with news" (kept exactly). The hook field avoids naming Sarah because the Qur'an does not; the script says Muslim tradition knows her as Sarah. Confirm.
"Slipped away to his household quietly" renders fa-ragha ila ahlihi (51:26); "so the guests wouldn't feel like a burden" is a common commentary explanation, stated as such. Confirm wording.
Fear at guests who won't eat: explained as a custom of the time (a guest refusing food might mean harm). This is the usual tafsir explanation; confirm.

Why Sarah laughed: the Qur'an's order in 11:71 puts the laugh before the news is stated; commentators differ (relief at the news about Lut's people, surprise, etc.). Script says only that they disagree.
Hadith number for honoring the guest cited from memory (Bukhari 6018/6019; Muslim 47); please confirm.
